summary: Provides information on profiling ISO 10646 for practical use, including restrictions on characters and combinations and the addition of language information. It also describes the charset ISO-10646-J-1 for Japanese use.

eli5.summary: The giant alphabet of every language has too many letters for some uses. This memo picks a sensible subset for Japanese.

questions: how to profile iso 10646 for japanese
subtitle: Simplifying a universal character set for practical use by restricting it.

tldr.problem: ISO 10646 is a universal character set that covers every language, but it is too large and complex for practical use. Different implementations need different subsets and restrictions.
tldr.mechanism: This memo defines two profiles: ISO-10646 (a minimal basic subset with Latin characters only) and ISO-10646-J-1 (a subset useful for Japanese that includes Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Japanese characters and mathematical symbols).
tldr.outcome: The memo provides recommended charset names for MIME to let email clients know which characters are supported, but the RFC notes these charsets should not be used for practical communication.

facts.label: ISO-10646-J-1 coverage
facts.value: Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, CJK symbols, Japanese Hiragana/Katakana, CJK ideographs

today: RFC 1815 is an Informational memo. It defines reference profiles for ISO 10646, but advises strongly against practical use of these charsets. ISO-2022-JP remains the preferred charset for Japanese email communication.

sections.title: Why Profiling Is Needed
sections.content:
ISO 10646 specifies every character in every major human language in a single 16-bit encoding, but it does not specify how implementations should handle character display, combining characters, or right-to-left text. Without restrictions, different systems display the same text differently or cannot display it at all.

The memo lists several practical problems: systems may have fonts for only a subset of characters (for example, Japanese Windows/NT has fonts for Japanese characters from JIS X 0208 only); combining characters require language-specific ordering rules; and bidirectional text (used by Arabic and Hebrew) needs special handling that ISO 10646 does not define. The solution is to define profiles, or restricted versions, of ISO 10646 for specific use cases.
sections.eli5: A universal alphabet is great in theory, but nobody has all the fonts, and different languages arrange their special symbols differently.

sections.title: Two Profiles Defined
sections.content:
The memo defines two profiles. ISO-10646 is the minimal basic profile containing only Latin characters (ASCII and Latin-1 Supplement, positions 0020-00FF in ISO 10646). It is simple, widely supported, and can be used with implementation level 1 (no combining characters).

ISO-10646-J-1 is tailored for Japanese. It includes Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, mathematical operators, CJK symbols, Japanese Hiragana and Katakana, and CJK Unified Ideographs, but only those characters present in JIS X 0208, the standard for Japanese data interchange. This ensures that Japanese Windows/NT systems can display the text, but it means the charset cannot display Chinese or Korean characters outside JIS X 0208.
sections.eli5: One profile is just the basic Latin alphabet. Another is the same plus everything a Japanese computer would have fonts for.

sections.title: Design Constraints and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo notes several constraints that shaped the design. Combining characters are excluded from both profiles until restrictions on combining order are standardized for each language. Bidirectional text support is excluded from the basic profile because it requires complex mechanisms not yet widely implemented. CJK character restrictions are necessary because different languages need different Han character shapes: Chinese uses one shape, Japanese uses another, and Korean uses a third. Adding language information (as the J-1 in ISO-10646-J-1 indicates) is the workaround.

The authors emphasize that these profiles are for reference purposes only and that using ISO 10646 for practical communication is strongly discouraged. Other charsets like ISO-2022-JP are better for Japanese communication.
sections.eli5: The memo lists hard problems that made simple solutions impossible, so it settles for something imperfect but workable.

sections.title: MIME Charset Names and Encoding
sections.content:
Both profiles encode text in 16-bit big-endian form. The RFC defines the charset names as iso-10646 and iso-10646-j-1 for use in MIME Content-Type headers, allowing email clients to understand what characters are supported. Since 16-bit encoding is binary, MIME messages using these charsets should use Base64 Content-Transfer-Encoding.

The profiles can also be used in MIME header extensions (RFC 1522), again with Base64 encoding.
sections.eli5: Email systems use these charset names to know which letters a message contains, and Base64 encoding to ship the 16-bit data safely.
